analytic.title: Evolving the Airborne Warning and Control System AWACS

div.p: We give an overview of ongoing development e orts and supporting research which is evolving the United States Air Force's Airborne Warning and Control System AWACS. AWACS is an airplane-based sensor and command and control platform with an on-board mission computing system that presents operators with sensor and other information subject to real-time quality of service r equirements. The legacy mission computing system is mainframe-based and relies on a centralized, cyclic scheduling approach which makes maintenance and improvement very di cult. We brie y discuss interesting aspects of our e orts to upgrade this system to use emerging real-time distributed object technology, object management, and modern scheduling and schedulability analysis. Advance demonstrations of this upgrade have been very successful, and test ights should be underway at the time of the conference. Within this context, we give examples of technology transfer.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The Airborne Warning and Control System AWACS includes sensors, radios for exchanging digital messages, operators maintaining situational awareness of the activities in the area, and a mission computing system which links these together. The mission computing system processes sensor reports, displays situational awareness information to operators, manages the exchange of messages with other platforms, and records mission data to disk. These functions have complex, dynamically varying real-time quality of service requirements, such as end-to-end deadlines, task priorities based on data element v alues, and periodic behavior. We quickly found that the techniques used in the legacy system were inadequate for upgrading AWACS.

We w ere able to meet these challenges by piecing together Air Force-sponsored research at MITRE and the University of Rhode Island, advanced technology demonstrations by MITRE and the Air Force Research Labs formerly, Rome Labs, standardization efforts being pursued by the Object Management Group OMG, and development e orts by Boeing, Lockheed Martin, Hazeltine, and Lincoln Labs. Our research and eventual development i n volves three technologies:

The real-time Common Object Request Broker Architecture CORBA being de ned by OMG for real-time, distributed communication and for definition of distributed computing services. Modern scheduling approaches, such as ratemonotonic methods, as applied to distributed, object-oriented systems. Real-time object management and concurrency control.

Each of these items is described in a section of this paper. These topics give a brief overview of the research and development to date, from the point of view of technology transfer. We conclude with a brief description of future work and sharing our results with other acquisitions.

div.head: Real-Time CORBA
div.p: The Object Management Group OMG, with participation from our team, is de ning a set of standards for a real-time Common Object Request Broker Architecture 7 . These standards extend the behavior of the Object Request Broker ORB, which is responsible for exible communication between CORBA components that may run on di erent platforms and may be implemented in di erent programming languages.

We c hose real-time CORBA as our infrastructure, even though it had yet to be de ned, because of positive experimental results and because of the wide variety o f domains that are participating in the e ort.

Our real-time CORBA approach is quite simple. We have implemented an ORB which uses OMG's Internet Inter-Orb Protocol IIOP for communication over the bre channel network being added to the AWACS aircraft. The choice to implement IIOP rather than a propriety protocol is intended to allow A WACS applications to inter-operate with other CORBA-based systems.

We further used CORBA and real-time CORBA standards to implement several services. First, we implemented an Event Service according to the associated OMG standard which allows asynchronous, event-style communication b e t ween components. Next, we implemented a Scheduling Service, which allows software components to interact with the real-time operating system's scheduling services see Section 2. Our use of the Scheduling Service allows us to study each component separately, and work is underway t o v alidate the temporal behavior of the upgraded system.

The AWACS mission computing system manages concurrent access to a large number of objects, so we de ned an Object Manager that uses the ORB for distributed communication and that uses the Object Database Management Group's ODMG's Object Description Language ODL 6 , which is an extension of CORBA's Interface Description Language IDL. The AWACS Object Manager is described in Section 3.

Meanwhile, we participated in ongoing OMG e orts to de ne standards for these and other real-time services. We w ere able to incorporate this emerging realtime CORBA technology into the evolution of AWACS partly because of the promising standards de nition and commercial product developments in the area. The team considered many possible approaches for improving the mission computing system on a limited budget, and selected CORBA and a distributed object philosophy to meet the user requirements. Although we c hose to implement our own ORB work done by L o c kheed Martin, we expect our ORB to be o ered as a commercial product in the future. In addition, other vendors are beginning to o er products appropriate for realtime avionics systems.

div.head: Scheduling and Temporal Analysis
div.p: The original scheduling policy for the AWACS data processing computer, which is still in use today i n t h e eet, is a classic cyclic executive running on a mainframe. This executive is based on a single-CPU xedexecution-order of AWACS functions such as surveillance, weapons control, and communications. This execution is logically grouped into three minor cycles that repeat every seven to ten seconds to complete a major cycle. Within each minor cycle, the executive s c hedules the tasks in a xed order, which i s de ned at build time. Most tasks execute every minor cycle, some execute only in a particular minor cycle, and some execute only when requested. Tasks performing output to communications channels and those handling some console operator inputs interrupt regular cyclic processing and execute to completion. Synchronization of the tasks, is in general, implicitly de ned by the order in which they execute 3 .

While the above technique was a fairly standard approach during the time in which A WACS was developed, it does su er from some fairly serious de ciencies. First, coupling between tasks can be implicit which can lead to ripple e ects" once the software reaches a maintenance phase. For example, the maintainer can see that Task A occurred prior to Task B but does not know i f A had to occur prior to B. If, due to software growth that causes a task to exceed its timing budget, Task A has to be split into two tasks, it can be very di cult to determine how that may impact Task B.

Second, there is no model that can be relied upon to determine the order of execution of tasks. For a system the size of AWACS, relying on a trial and error assignment of execution order can be a costly decision. Third, what happens when a task overruns its budgeted time? The granularity of pre-emption a minor cycle is larger than is desired for modern, responsive systems. Finally, what happens when the external world, and thus the stimulus for the work, includes multiple cycles and sporadic events?

The AWACS Program O ce decided to take proactive measures to ensure that the platform could continue to perform its mission in the next century. A decision was made to move from a cyclic executive t o a more exible approach that should result in lower cost changes that can be elded more quickly yet still have the platform behave in a predictable manner. In order to investigate the risks involved in moving away from a main-frame based cyclic executive strategy, the AWACS project o ce supported, and the Air Force Research Lab funded, an e ort by MITRE to prototype an infrastructure with a more robust scheduling mechanism.

To a c hieve these goals, it was decided to gradually migrate AWACS functions to new PowerPC computers, which will eventually allow the mainframe-based system to be retired. The scheduling of tasks on these new computers is being designed now. The approach is to use a static, pre-emptive priority driven scheme in conjunction with a commercial real-time operating system. The priorities will be assigned based on a rate monotonic analysis 5 .

The strengths of rate monotonic scheduling are well known. Given valid assumptions, highly predictable behavior can be obtained. Unfortunately, these assumptions can be very di cult to validate especially for large complex systems such as a modern military Command and Control platform. For example, the worst case loading and the maximum execution times can be very di cult to determine and, in fact, change over the life of a system due to modi cations in the concepts of operations and modi cations to the system applications.

Thus, while AWACS is being upgraded now to use the static, pre-emptive priority driven approach, the Program O ce has been supporting an investigation into whether an adaptive, dynamic scheduling approach might prove useful. At the very least, it is hoped that this investigation will yield useful results for situations in which rate monotonic assumptions have been violated.

This activity is a collaboration between the AWACS Program O ce, The MITRE Corporation, Air Force Research Laboratory Rome, NY, and the Open Group Research Institute. The goal of this e ort is to investigate the use of a scalable, evolvable, real-time architecture that enables an application to adapt to anomalies such a s w ork overloads and hardware and software failures. Technologies being used to support this project include:

Quality of Service driven adaptive computing Dynamic scheduling of tasks Migrating threads of execution The use of a dynamic real-time scheduling strategy was chosen due to its potential to be more applicable for the dynamic external and internal AWACS environment. Note that internal changes are becoming increasingly more important for military systems due to the goal of signi cantly reducing the time it takes to modify a system and the recognition that a mission computing system consists of certain relatively xed assets, such as an airframe and numerous loosely and tightly coupled hardware and software components. It is rare to nd a system that is being built today with exact knowledge of the required capabilities, at least beyond the immediate future.

The policy being examined on this activity is called Best-E ort Scheduling 4 . Best-E ort Scheduling is attractive because it considers both the time constraints associated with a piece of work and the value accrued by the system in completing this work.

Best-E ort Scheduling employ s a t wo phase approach. The scheduler tries rst to schedule the work using an Earliest Deadline First EDF algorithm. EDF is optimal in the sense of feasibility and it also minimizes the maximum lateness 1 . If not all deadlines can be met, then load is shed based on the lowest value density u n til the remaining tasks deadlines can be met.

Value is de ned by use of time-value functions. These functions, whose shape can vary over time, represent the value of completing a task. This is useful to the system designer because the combination of EDF and time-value functions allows scheduling decisions to be based on both the timing requirements and the relative importances of the tasks.

For our investigation, we are using the best e ort algorithm to control the execution of a airborne surveillance tracking application. The application was designed so that there are multiple tracking threads. The value functions of these threads are dynamically dened and are based on attributes such as the importance of the track and sensor data and the quality o f the current track estimates.

This investigation is still ongoing, but the initial results are encouraging. During simulation runs, the system is able to handle severe overloads and, through the adaptive s c heduling approach, still not drop tracks. In addition, early results from the prototype indicate similar behavior. Important tracks are receiving higher quality of service but less important tracks still receive some level of service.

The developed prototype will be evaluated by the AWACS operational community in the Fall of 1998. Based in part on this evaluation, a technology transfer plan will be developed for incorporation of this adaptive technology into AWACS.

div.head: Object Management
div.p: Our early research recognized that software is needed to manage access by system components to the objects that represent the essential functionality of AWACS mission computing 3 . However, we s o o n found that existing commercial products and developing standards did not meet our needs, and research w as needed to consider the application of work in real-time databases, real-time scheduling, and object databases. We performed some initial research i n to semantic locking, in which concurrency control can be adapted to the the needs of the application by identifying the methods of an object that can be executed concurrently. W e also investigated algorithms that respect the priorities of tasks which execute transactions 8 . These ideas led to the implementation of an Object Manager for AWACS which respects task priorities but does not yet apply our concurrency control research.

This area of technology transfer is only beginning. In the rst phase of AWACS evolution, most data will remain under the control of the legacy system, so object management capabilities have not yet become the focus of the development. Some initial investigations have shown that the AWACS Object Manager can meet the needs of our applications if concurrency control and real-time scheduling requirements can be managed appropriately. W e are continuing to investigate this issue and plan to transfer this work to the AWACS program.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: We h a ve found that research and prototyping of realtime software infrastructure can be successfully transferred to a deployed system. However, bigger bene ts can be realized by reusing such results across multiple acquisitions. We h a ve begun sharing these technologies with other similar development e orts, which includes describing the techniques used to architects and developers, and surveying our program costs and risks to managers and users. Due to this kind of information sharing, we h a ve been able to submit our infrastructure software to the Defense Information Infrastructure's Common Operational Environment COE 2 , which is an emerging e ort to share and standardize software across US Department of Defense DoD programs.

COE provides for sharing of approved software congurations across DoD. We began by recommending commercial real-time operating systems to COE based on our experience. We h a ve also submitted our realtime CORBA ORB, scheduling service, and object manager to COE as infrastructure software. We plan to submit further AWACS components in the future as shared mission applications. These e orts allow costs to be shared across many acquisitions and enhance the impacts of technology transfer.
